London UCL Clear Speech in Interaction
LUCID: adult conversations collected by Rachel Baker and Valerie Hazan at UCL
40 adults aged 18–29 spoke southern British English.
Pairs described pictures to find differences without seeing each other’s picture.
Listening conditions included normal conversation, background voices, vocoded sound and a partner learning English.
The corpus contains audio and human transcripts with words, timestamps and speaker labels.
We chose it to check our vocabulary calculations against existing reference values.

Corpus materials come from SpeechBox at Northwestern University. Full corpus also includes sentence reading and picture naming, which we did not use for this dialogue comparison. Vocoded listening simulates aspects of cochlear-implant listening. The downloaded TextGrid README explains stereo Speaker A/B tiers and the sole target-native-speaker tier for L2.
LUCID: the files and reference values
Downloaded human transcripts: 300 Praat TextGrid files from SpeechBox.
Retained reference file: TAALED_results.csv, recorded as the paper’s OSF export. It has 240 samples and 40 speaker IDs.
Each reference condition contains 20 speakers and three scenes per speaker.
We scored 180 samples. The other 60 have ambiguous vocoder recording matches.
The local file matches saved acquisition metadata. Independent confirmation against the author-hosted file is still pending.

Separate corpus creators from later lexical analysts: Melissa Baese-Berk and colleagues reused LUCID in2021 and shared TAALED/TAALES exports and R analysis code. Footnote2 and the Data availability statement link OSF. Current download attempts failed; local metadata alone cannot independently authenticate the historical transfer. Preserve all files and numerical results as provisional for publication. There are60 babble,60 L2,60 noBarrier and120 vocoder TextGrids. No sample is chosen by closeness to a reference score.
Wagner and colleagues, 2025. Available through TalkBank CHILDES.
The published corpus contains 303 children, ages 4–9.
Researchers recorded speech in a science-museum language lab in Ohio.
We use the children’s human CHAT transcripts.
We selected picture descriptions and “how to” explanations: 301 children and 803 task sections.
This provides a larger child-speech reference for testing utterance measures.

Selected gems: ExpPictures, Howto, DescriptivePictures. Reading, alphabet, number and Wug tasks remain outside the selected discourse preparation. Two source children have no eligible discourse section. Source media include lapel-microphone audio. Published age range is4–9; local CHAT age-header minimum differs, so development medians are explicitly header-derived.
New York University and Emerson College
Parent–child interaction corpus, available through TalkBank ASDBank
The released corpus contains 30 autistic children. Recruitment targeted ages 3 to under 6.
Families completed play and conversation, mainly over Zoom at home.
We use the child’s human CHAT transcript from free play, pretend play and sensory play.
28 children contribute 92 usable task sections. Two have too little eligible speech for boundary scoring.
We chose it to test transfer to young autistic children. The source also provides video.

Official corpus title is NYU–Emerson Corpus. Expanded institution names are used on slides at the user’s request. Citation: Steen, Buonocore, Luyster, Sancimino and Arunachalam2026. The current release contains30 autistic children, not the larger parent-study sample. Two excluded sources remain assigned to original train but supply no prepared records.
All sections from a child stay in that child’s original cohort.

The model receives words and observed speaker turns.
Human utterance endings stay in the reference used for comparison.

Same five-step abstraction as the simplified Excalidraw pipeline. Detailed implementation: lexical calculations use the historical TAALED compatibility branch; predicted utterances export faithful CHAT and native CLAN computes surface measures. The retained workflow is turn_ml, margin0.25. Human utterance cuts are withheld at inference. Consecutive same-speaker human rows merge into observed turns; that context remains available.

The model is a pretrained encoder with task-specific learned components, fine-tuned jointly. Architecture: MiniLM-L12-H384-uncased,16-dimensional rule embedding and128-unit GELU/dropout gap classifier. Historical TAALED conventions are a fixed software profile, not a model trained on LUCID. Current spaCy software remains in use; historical environment was not reconstructed exactly.
Percentage error describes the difference from the reference. Lower is better.

We calculate absolute percentage error per sample, then average within participants and across participants.

APE=100*abs(predicted-reference)/abs(reference). Undefined/zero denominators remain missing. Native FREQ and MLU have different word eligibility. Eligible count differs from all verbal units. LUCID uses per-recording values, then speaker averaging. Our percentage errors and engineering targets are our evaluation outputs, not paper-reported model accuracy.
Aligned vocabulary processing with historical TAALED dictionary, word-category and pause rules.
Used native CLAN calculations to respect CHAT word and utterance eligibility.
Compared prediction from whole paragraphs, prediction within observed speaker turns, and rules.
Tested fixed settings for deciding where utterances end on development participants.
Compared learning rates and count-loss weights using five-fold participant cross-validation.

Earlier production selection favored observed-turn ML, margin0.25. An initial batching inconsistency was caught and calibration reran through original preprocessing with exact parity checks. A single-evaluation ensemble branch was superseded by the participant-CV search. The fourth training configuration stopped in fold1. The lexical and native-scoring changes did not rewrite source words. No new final fit or activation occurred after the user stopped further experiments.

TAALED=Tool for the Automatic Analysis of Lexical Diversity, developed by Kristopher Kyle with Scott Crossley and Scott Jarvis. Baese-Berk etal2021 used TAALED diversity and TAALES sophistication, and shared an OSF export and R analysis script. The local reference identity requires independent reconfirmation before publication. We did not reproduce TAALES outputs, figure4 moving-average MTLD, mixed-model coefficients or p-values. Babble and the English-learner condition show close agreement. No-barrier word counts remain less consistent.
Vocoder recording matches are unresolved. Independent author-source confirmation is also pending.

The English-learner partner condition is coded L2 in the reference file. Each scored condition includes60 samples from20 speakers. All240 local reference rows remain visible in coverage. All15 shared means meet project engineering targets in babble/L2, but those thresholds are internal goals, not clinical standards. No-barrier discrepancies may include source matching and preparation differences. These are lexical transcript comparisons, not ASR or boundary-model accuracy.

The parent–child corpus provides shorter contexts, more missing speech and much less training text.
Age, task and coding vary together. These observations do not establish age as the cause.

Profiles use original train+eval only. Training words5336 vs229378; native reference FREQ/MLU word-total gaps7.22% vs1.79%. NYU has more masked supervision near unintelligibility. Corpus-balanced sampling does not create additional independent children. BoundaryF1 in preceding CV wasNYU88.81% vsOhio87.22%, so the difficulty is metric-specific. LUCID checks a different lexical component; no-barrier discrepancies may involve source/preparation differences and vocoder matching remains ambiguous.
One Ohio Child Speech Corpus picture-description section, 300 seconds
The pilot used MOSS transcription, a frozen MiniLM model and native CLAN.
Speaker-role matching used the human reference. Automatic child identification and cohort accuracy still need evaluation.

Existing saved pilot, not a new run. OCSC4002 ExpPictures,300.021s. ChildWER18.8172% uses oracle minimum-edit role mapping after ASR, not reference text supplied to generation. Native metric rowlatest_minilm_native_clan. Reference72utterances/179words versus predicted70/174 gives near-identical MLU ratios; small MLU error alone does not establish general accuracy. Reported SD/MATTR retain native three-decimal precision. Saved raw output and audio hashes match the manifest/evaluation. Keep this single-recording evidence separate from participant test summaries.
Use the same child, recording and task section in both paths.
Measure word recognition errors separately from vocabulary and utterance-measure errors.

ASR=automatic speech recognition. Future multi-participant evaluation extends the earlier feasibility pilot. Review target-speaker/channel mapping, time intervals, privacy edits and word eligibility before scoring. Preserve cohort assignments. Use human transcripts to measure word error rate, then downstream language-measure differences. This slide describes planned work, not completed cohort audio results.
